query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing that refines the lamellar colonies into an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure will improve both the strength and room-temperature tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with conventional lamellar-colony microstructures featuring continuous internal boundaries that promote microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermo-mechanical processing route (e.g., optimized rolling and annealing) to induce an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure while preserving the lamellar architecture.
generation.conditions: The processing parameters must be tuned to prevent grain coarsening (e.g., avoiding excessive annealing) and to ensure the desired hierarchical phase distribution in alloys such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure with engineered, robust phase boundaries that act as sites for microcrack deflection and arrest.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement increases dislocation accumulation and promotes a two-tiered constraint effect. The improved distribution and strengthened phase boundaries arrest microcrack propagation, thereby enhancing both strength (through dislocation strengthening) and ductility (via delayed crack growth).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the processed alloy is expected to have higher yield strength and greater tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing that produces coarse lamellar colonies with continuous internal boundaries, leading to microcracking and limited ductility.
generation.boundary: This approach is effective only if the processing parameters successfully yield a refined duplex microstructure without introducing over-annealing effects that could cause softening or other defects; its effectiveness may also depend on the specific alloy system used.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing conditions for achieving the ideal hierarchical microstructure and the degree of improvement across different eutectic high-entropy alloy compositions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an EHEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1): one via conventional casting and one with the tailored thermo-mechanical processing. Conduct detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., via SEM/TEM) to verify the microstructural refinement and duplex structure, then perform room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase boundary characteristics (using SEM/TEM)
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture from tensile tests
In situ or post-mortem analysis of microcrack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility compared to the conventional baseline, or if the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure is not observed or does not correlate with improved crack arrest behavior, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
